title: CPU, GPU, TPU, and NPU Compared at a Glance
reading_goal: Instead of memorizing them separately, students understand the differences in the roles of these computational devices as a single concept.
code:
CPU: 범용 계산, 복잡한 분기, 운영체제/일반 프로그램 실행에 강함
GPU: 많은 코어로 같은 연산을 대량 병렬 처리, 행렬/벡터 연산에 강함
TPU: 구글이 만든 딥러닝 행렬 연산 특화 가속기
NPU: 기기나 SoC 안에서 AI 추론을 빠르고 저전력으로 처리하는 가속기
question: Which of the following best describes a GPU?
choices: It can only run the operating system
Perform document OCR exclusively on Google Cloud
It excels at mass parallel processing of operations of the same type
answer: It excels at mass parallel processing of operations of the same type
explanation: GPUs excel at tasks that involve repeating the same calculations many times, such as matrix multiplication, image processing, and deep learning. CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs each excel at different types of computations. As a general rule, think of CPUs for conditional branching and general-purpose tasks, and GPUs or dedicated accelerators for massively parallel computations.
project_context: This is a basic comparison to help understand why `cuda/device/batch_size` appears in AI code.

title: Tasks the CPU Is Well-Suited For
reading_goal: Understand that the CPU excels at general-purpose control and complex branching.
question: What kind of device does this code most closely resemble?
explanation: Complex branching, I/O coordination, and various types of task control are tasks best handled by the CPU. The CPU plays a central role in sequentially processing a variety of tasks, such as condition evaluation, file processing, and flow control. It is easier to understand this by comparing the nature of these tasks with those handled by the GPU.
project_context: The logic of the batch pipeline, collector, and server consists mostly of CPU control flow.

title: Tasks Best Suited for a GPU
reading_goal: I understand that GPUs are good at processing large numbers of calculations simultaneously.
code:
import torch

a = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda")
b = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda")
c = a @ b
question: Why is this code well-suited for the GPU?
choices: Because there are so many if/else statements
Because it is well-suited for parallel processing of large matrix multiplications
answer: Because it is well-suited for parallel processing of large matrix multiplications
explanation: GPUs excel at processing large numbers of calculations in parallel. Since deep learning models involve a large number of matrix and tensor operations, GPU acceleration is highly effective. It is easier to determine the reason for using a GPU by examining whether the code repeats the same operations on a large amount of data. Therefore, the correct answer is “because it is well-suited for processing large matrix multiplications in parallel.”
project_context: This ties into the reason for moving tensors to CUDA in PyTorch.

title: Understanding the TPU Concept
reading_goal: Understand that TPU is a device specialized for deep learning matrix operations.
code:
# TPU는 일반 파이썬 문법이 아니라 딥러닝 연산을 빠르게 처리하는 가속기다.
# 보통 클라우드/프레임워크 설정과 함께 등장한다.
question: Which of the following best describes TPU?
choices: An accelerator specialized for deep learning matrix operations
answer: An accelerator specialized for deep learning matrix operations
explanation: TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit and is an accelerator designed to quickly process deep learning computations. The TPU is an AI-specific accelerator developed by Google. It is optimized for matrix operations, deep learning training, and inference, and the criteria for selecting a TPU may differ from those for a GPU.
project_context: Although it is an accelerator similar to a GPU, it is primarily found in specific deep learning workloads and cloud environments.

title: Understanding the Concept of NPU
reading_goal: I understand that NPUs are widely used for accelerating on-device AI inference and low-power processing.
code: # NPUs are frequently used to perform AI inference quickly and with low power consumption in smartphones, laptops, and embedded devices.
question: Which of the following best describes an NPU?
choices: A device that accelerates AI inference within a device while maintaining low power consumption
answer: A device that accelerates AI inference within a device while maintaining low power consumption
explanation: NPU stands for Neural Processing Unit and is frequently mentioned in the context of on-device AI inference. An NPU is a dedicated processor designed to quickly process AI computations. Its role differs from that of a CPU or GPU, and it is primarily used for inference optimization or low-power AI execution. Therefore, the correct answer is “a device that accelerates AI inference within a device while consuming low power.”
project_context: This is necessary for understanding the AI capabilities of smartphones, laptops, and edge devices.

title: How the CPU and GPU Work Together
reading_goal: I understand the workflow where the CPU prepares the data and the GPU handles the computationally intensive tensor operations.
code:
# CPU side
text = load_text("prompt.txt")
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

# GPU side
inputs = {k: v.to("cuda") for k, v in inputs.items()}
outputs = model.generate(**inputs)
question: Which of the following best describes this code flow?
choices: The GPU reads the filename, and the CPU performs the matrix multiplication.
The NPU performs a Git push
The CPU prepares the text/input, and the GPU handles the model computations.
answer: The CPU prepares the text/input, and the GPU handles the model computations.
explanation: In an AI pipeline, the CPU and GPU share specific roles. The CPU is often responsible for data preparation and control, while the GPU handles computationally intensive tensor operations. Since moving data between the two devices incurs a cost, it is important to understand the workflow to determine when to send data to the GPU and when to retrieve it. Therefore, the result of this call-back is that “the CPU prepares the text or input, and the GPU handles the model computations.”
project_context: Understand why model inference is divided into data preparation and GPU computation.

title: CPU↔GPU Data Transfer Overhead
reading_goal: I understand that even when using a GPU, performance can slow down if data is moved frequently.
question: What is `batch.to('cuda')` most similar to?
choices: Move data from the CPU to GPU memory
answer: Move data from the CPU to GPU memory
explanation: Since CPU memory and GPU memory are separate spaces, transferring data incurs a cost. If there is more data transfer than computation, the overall speed may slow down. Since `batch.to('cuda')` transfers tensors to the GPU, you should also check whether it is being called too frequently within the loop.
project_context: If performance is slow even though you have a GPU, you should suspect a bottleneck in data transfer or preprocessing.

title: Operations Suitable for Parallel Processing
reading_goal: Read about why GPUs are advantageous when performing the same calculation repeatedly on large amounts of data.
code:
# many independent scores
scores = embeddings @ query_vector
question: Why is this operation well-suited for the GPU?
choices: Because the branching is very complex
Because the file path is long
Because it is waiting for user input
Because it allows you to calculate many vector scores at once
answer: Because it allows you to calculate many vector scores at once
explanation: Parallelism is a method of processing multiple computations simultaneously. Vector and matrix operations are well-suited for parallelization because they involve repeated computations of the same type. The more a problem can be broken down into many small, independent computations, the greater the benefits of parallel processing. Therefore, the correct answer is “because it allows for the simultaneous calculation of many vector scores.”
project_context: This is why vector search and embedding similarity calculations are well-suited for GPUs.

title: Code with many branches puts a load on the CPU
reading_goal: Understand that code with many if/else statements and a wide variety of tasks is closer to CPU control flow than to GPU control flow.
question: What kind of code is this?
choices: Branch and control code that is easy for the CPU to optimize
answer: Branch and control code that is easy for the CPU to optimize
explanation: GPUs excel at simple, repetitive, large-scale computations, while the CPU primarily handles this type of control flow. Code with many branches is easy to understand in terms of CPU flow because it involves frequent conditional checks. This can be distinguished from GPU-type tasks that involve repeating the same calculation a large number of times.
project_context: The batching, queuing, retry, and saving workflow may be a CPU bottleneck rather than a GPU bottleneck.

title: GPU Memory and Model Size
reading_goal: Understand that VRAM is affected by model size, input length, and batch size.
code:
# 큰 모델 + 긴 입력 + 큰 batch_size = 더 많은 VRAM 사용
batch_size = 8
max_length = 2048
question: If you get a "CUDA out of memory" error, what can you try reducing first?
explanation: VRAM usage is affected not only by model size but also by input length and batch size. GPU memory is the space where the model and batch data are stored. You need to determine how model size, batch size, and precision settings affect memory usage.
project_context: This is a skill that is often needed when running local LLMs and LoRAs.

title: Analysis When GPU Utilization Is Low
reading_goal: I understand that just because the GPU score appears low doesn't necessarily mean the GPU is slow.
question: What are some possible causes of low GPU utilization?
choices: It's always the GPU that breaks down.
This means that the model is always fast.
That means the internet is down.
CPU preprocessing, I/O, and small batches may be bottlenecks
answer: CPU preprocessing, I/O, and small batches may be bottlenecks
explanation: A low GPU utilization rate does not necessarily mean the GPU is slow. The GPU may be waiting for computations to begin due to data loading, CPU preprocessing, or disk I/O, creating a bottleneck. When evaluating performance, you should consider not only GPU utilization but also data preparation time and batch size.
project_context: This is necessary for troubleshooting when Node-Pass/batch jobs aren't running as fast as expected.

title: The Computational Difference Between Inference and Learning
reading_goal: Understand that inference is forward-only, while learning involves the addition of a backward pass and an optimizer.
code:
# inference
with torch.no_grad():
    output = model(x)

# training
loss = model(x).loss
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
question: What is the key flow found only in the learning code?
explanation: Training requires gradient calculation and parameter updates, so it consumes more memory and computational resources than inference. Inference is the process of generating an answer using a pre-trained model, while training is the process of adjusting the model’s weights. The computational requirements and the values that need to be stored differ between the two. Therefore, the correct answer is “loss.backward and optimizer.step.”
project_context: Understand the difference in resource requirements between LoRA training and local inference.

title: NPU and On-Device AI
reading_goal: I understand that, unlike server GPUs, NPUs are often used for low-power inference within devices.
code:
# phone/laptop side
# camera frame -> NPU inference -> result on device
question: In what situations is the NPU mentioned particularly often?
choices: When you're just making a Git commit
When performing AI inference on mobile phones, laptops, or Edge devices
answer: When performing AI inference on mobile phones, laptops, or Edge devices
explanation: An NPU is an accelerator designed to process AI computations in a power-efficient manner. It is commonly used in on-device AI, where power consumption and latency are critical factors. It’s easy to understand when you think of environments with significant battery and thermal constraints, such as smartphones or small devices. Therefore, the correct answer is “when performing AI inference on cell phones, laptops, or edge devices.”
project_context: This is necessary for understanding AI on PCs, AI on smartphones, and edge inference in robots.

title: TPU and Cloud Training/Inference
reading_goal: I understand that TPUs are often introduced in conjunction with specific frameworks or cloud environments.
code: # TPUs typically come with framework configurations, cloud runtimes, and dedicated libraries.
question: What other factors should you consider when looking at TPU?
explanation: Unlike a standard GPU, which can be used immediately with any code, you must first verify the supported environment for a TPU. A TPU is a device specialized for specific deep learning computations, and in the cloud, it is often used on a pay-as-you-go basis. You need to consider both the execution environment and cost conditions, rather than just the code itself.
project_context: It is helpful for comparing Colab and cloud AI environments.

title: A Sense of Choosing the Right Accelerator for Each Task
reading_goal: We compare the options to determine which device is best suited for the nature of the task.
code:
Workload examples:
- Many if/else + file I/O: CPU
- Large matrix multiplication: GPU/TPU
- On-device low-power inference: NPU
- General app logic + orchestration: CPU
question: What is the best choice for deep learning training that involves a large number of matrix-vector multiplications?
choices: Only a single core of the CPU
explanation: The choice of accelerator depends on the type of computation and operating conditions. When there are many large tensor and matrix operations, the advantages of parallel accelerators become particularly evident. To determine whether a GPU or NPU is better than a CPU, one must consider not only speed but also power consumption, memory, and deployment location. Therefore, the correct answer is “GPU or TPU.”
project_context: Develop an eye for choosing AI development environments and servers.

title: A GPU doesn't make all code run faster
reading_goal: I understand that just because you use a GPU doesn't mean all Python code automatically runs faster.
code:
# This loop is mostly Python/CPU control work.
for file in files:
    text = file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    rows.append(parse(text))
question: Why is it difficult to significantly speed up this code using only the GPU?
choices: Because there are too many matrix multiplications
Because the NPU handles it automatically
Because it focuses on file I/O and Python control flow
answer: Because it focuses on file I/O and Python control flow
explanation: While GPUs excel at tensor and matrix operations, file reading, branching, and parsing can create other bottlenecks. GPUs do not necessarily speed up all code. Code that contains tasks difficult to parallelize, file I/O, or numerous conditional branches may be better suited for the CPU. Therefore, the correct answer is “because file I/O and Python control flow are central to the code.”
project_context: It is important to analyze bottlenecks in batch job processing speeds.
